state.misconception_label: Thinks alternate angles are always equal

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are arguing about alternate angles. Tom says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate. Katie says angles \( p \) and \( q \) are equal. Who is correct? ![Shows two non parallel lines that are intersected by another line. Angles P and Q are both on the outside of the lines and on opposite sides of the transversal.](). I got Only
Katie because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you and a friend are playing a game of tag. You are on one side of the playground and your friend is on the other. When you both run towards each other and cross paths, you are like the intersecting lines in the diagram. The angles you make with each other, like angles \( p \) and \( q \), are alternate angles. But are they always equal?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get what you're saying about the game of tag and how the angles are like that. But if angles \( p \) and \( q \) are alternate angles, why aren't they always equal? I thought they were just because they're on opposite sides of the transversal. Can you explain that a bit more?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you and your friend are playing a game of catch instead of tag. When you throw the ball to each other, the distance you throw and catch from each other is like the measure of the angles. Just like how the distance you throw and catch can be different, the measure of alternate angles can also be different. So, alternate angles are not always equal, just like the distance you throw and catch the ball can vary.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get it a bit better now. So, alternate angles can be different, just like how you can throw the ball different distances. But what if the lines are parallel? Do the alternate angles then become equal, or is it still not guaranteed?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses vague analogies that don't directly address the parallel/non-parallel distinction central to the misconception, provides no reasoning opportunities, and the student's final question shows they still haven't grasped when alternate angles are equal versus when they aren't.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently grounds abstract geometric concepts in concrete, relatable real-world scenarios (playground tag game, throwing a ball) to help the student understand alternate angles and their properties.
